facts.text: The little wattlebird is also known as the brush wattlebird.
facts.quote: The little wattlebird (Anthochaera chrysoptera), also known as the brush wattlebird, is a passerine bird in the honeyeater family Meliphagidae.

facts.text: Despite its name, the little wattlebird lacks the wattles that characterise other members of its genus.
facts.quote: The little wattlebird lacks the wattles, which characterise other members of the genus.

facts.text: Its calls include a strident cookay-cok and a raucous 'fetch the gun'.
facts.quote: Calls include a strident cookay-cok, a raucous fetch the gun, a mellow guttural yekkop, yekkop and many squeaky, musical lilting notes.

facts.text: Breeding takes place from June to December.
facts.quote: Breeding takes place from June to December.

facts.text: The female builds a loose, untidy cup nest of twigs placed 1 to 10 m high in a banksia, tea-tree or eucalypt sapling.
facts.quote: The female wattlebird generally constructs the nest, which is a loose, untidy cup of twigs, lined with shredded bark, and placed from 1 to 10 m high in the fork of a banksia, tea-tree or eucalypt sapling.

facts.text: Its 1-2 eggs may be spotted red-brown, purplish-red or salmon-pink.
facts.quote: 1-2 eggs are laid and may be spotted red-brown, purplish-red or salmon-pink in colour.

facts.text: It feeds on nectar using a long, brush-tipped tongue adapted for probing deep into flowers.
facts.quote: Little wattlebirds feed on nectar obtained with a long, brush-tipped tongue, adapted for probing deep into flowers.

facts.text: It eats insects, berries and some seeds, and can catch insects in mid-air.
facts.quote: They also feed on insects, berries, and some seeds. Most feeding is done perched, but some insects are caught in mid-air.

facts.text: It lives in banksia and eucalypt woodlands, heathlands and even parks and gardens.
facts.quote: The little wattlebird is found in banksia/eucalypt woodlands, heathlands, tea-tree scrub, sandplain-heaths, lantana thickets, wild tobacco, parks and gardens.
